overview: British administrators combined northern and southern protectorates into colonial Nigeria in 1914, joining many older societies without their consent. A tiny property-qualified electorate got a limited vote in 1922. Farmers and traders supplied cocoa, palm produce, groundnuts and cotton; women’s market networks also organized major protests. Yoruba newspapers, carving and woven cloth reveal creative life beyond colonial offices. Schools and health programmes grew unevenly. Nigeria became independent in 1960, not at the imported map’s 1938 endpoint.

periods.title: Colonial union and public resistance
periods.summary: British amalgamation brought separate regions under one government. Limited voting, export farming, print culture and women’s protests shaped the period.

periods.title: Regional self-government and independence
periods.summary: Nigerian campaigns won broader representation and regional autonomy. Women challenged taxes; regional schools expanded before independence in 1960.

sections.title: A new colonial border, older peoples

items.text: In 1914 British rule joined the northern and southern protectorates. The new territory contained communities with much older histories, including kingdoms, emirates and towns. Amalgamation made a colonial administration; it did not invent the people.

The 1922 constitution offered just four elected legislative seats, three for Lagos and one for Calabar, with an income requirement that shut out most people. A small ballot box was not national self-government.

Colonial marketing boards bought and graded cocoa, palm produce, groundnuts and cotton. Which crop mattered to a household varied widely by region, while export prices were set in a larger imperial market.

Political changes in the 1950s gave regions more autonomy. On 1 October 1960 Nigeria became independent; in 1963 it adopted a republic. Neither date means all regional arguments or colonial inequalities vanished.

sections.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse

items.text: In southeastern Ngwa communities women cultivated and processed palm produce, sold kernels and helped pay household bills. When tax assessment threatened their autonomy in 1929, women organized what is remembered as the Women’s War, rather than waiting for colonial officials to speak for them.

In Abeokuta, the Women’s Union led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti challenged taxes and colonial-era authority in the 1940s. Food prices, trade and political rights belonged to the same household conversation.

Lagos readers could find politics, sports, medicine advertisements, proverbs and serialized stories in Yoruba newspapers. Akede Eko was a weekly from 1928. A newspaper was both news and something to talk about with neighbors.

“Itan Igbesi-Aiye Emi” means “The story of my life.” These original Yoruba words open the title of I. B. Thomas’s Segilola story, serialized in Akede Eko from 1929 to 1930. They show a written language and a playful, sometimes controversial popular fiction, not a colonial decree.

The Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved extraordinary palace doors in the early twentieth century, showing a royal visit by British officials. A 1920s indigo aso oke wrap shows narrow handwoven cotton strips, silk and careful stitching. These are specific artworks, not a single national dress.

Western Nigeria began free primary schooling in 1955; Eastern Nigeria and Lagos expanded programmes in 1957. Children’s opportunities varied by region, fees, gender and available teachers, so a new school promise did not mean an identical classroom everywhere.

Lagos health officials made mobile films in the 1930s about malaria, baby health and even building latrines. The films show that sanitation mattered, but they do not prove every household had a safe toilet. Audiences could laugh at or challenge a film as well as learn from it.

A family’s access to a clinic, clean water or a latrine depended on town, income and colonial priorities. The government’s own health-film campaign treated these as problems needing work, not services already solved.

Commercial oil was found at Oloibiri in 1956, just before independence. It would transform government revenue but eventually raise difficult questions about the land and water of Niger Delta communities.

ending.text: On 1 October 1960 the colonial territory became an independent federal state. The republic followed in 1963. People, languages and local institutions continued across independence, while debates about federal power, resources, schooling and colonial legacies remained. The imported 1938 map endpoint is not the date Britain left.

sources.note: British conquest and January 1914 amalgamation; colonial administration through independence in 1960.

sources.note: Many earlier kingdoms, states and communities predated the 1914 colonial state.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Palm Oil and Protest: Women Riot 1929
sources.note: Original historical research on Ngwa women’s palm production, household spending, tax fears and the 1929 Women’s War.

sources.title: Cambridge History in Africa, The Lost Province
sources.note: Original research notes Igbo term Ogu Umunwanyi, Women’s War, for 1929 protest; modern scholarly usage.

sources.title: UNESCO, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and the Women’s Union of Abeokuta
sources.note: Abeokuta Women’s Union mobilized tens of thousands for women’s rights and anticolonial politics.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Women, Rice, and War in Abeokuta
sources.note: Original research traces wartime food controls, women’s trade and 1947 Abeokuta tax revolt.

sources.title: University of Ibadan, Akede Eko Newspaper Collection
sources.note: Primary Yoruba newspaper issues include political reports, medicines, sports, reader letters, proverbs and cultural writing.

sources.title: Osaka University, Yoruba-Language Newspapers in Colonial Lagos
sources.note: Original press research identifies Akede Eko (The Lagos Herald), published 1928–53, and the 1920s Yoruba print boom.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Alaroye and Yoruba Newspaper Culture
sources.note: Original scholarship on I. B. Thomas’s 1929–30 Yoruba serial about Segilola and Akede Eko; title begins Itan Igbesi-Aiye Emi (Story of My Life).

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Olowe of Ise Palace Door
sources.note: Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved Ise palace doors around 1904–10 portraying royal and colonial visitors; named artist and patron.

sources.title: British Museum, Aso Oke Cloth from Nigeria
sources.note: 1920–30 Yoruba narrow-strip indigo cotton wrap with silk stripes and hand stitching; material evidence of textile skill and regional exchange.

sources.title: Nigerian Federal Ministry of Education, Education Sector Status Report
sources.note: Western Region began universal primary education 1955; Eastern and Lagos in 1957; opportunities and fees differed across regions; University College Ibadan 1948.

sources.title: National Library of Nigeria, Department of Marketing and Exports Annual Report 1950–51
sources.note: Colonial government marketing boards dealt with cocoa, oil-palm produce, groundnuts and cotton; exports reflected different farming regions.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Audience Responses to Colonial Health Films
sources.note: Original research on 1930s Lagos health films, mobile screenings and latrine-construction films; audiences did not simply accept colonial messages.

sources.title: NNPC Limited, History of Oil at Oloibiri
sources.note: First commercial oil discovery at Oloibiri in 1956, before independence.

sources.title: UNEP, Environmental Assessment of Ogoniland
sources.note: 2011 independent assessment linked long oil operations to contaminated drinking water, land and mangroves in Ogoniland.
